t: Introduction: topic, aim and sources
n: In this lecture we consider patients' rights and ethics committees. The patients' rights movement began in the 1970s. In 1972 the American Hospital Association adopted the “Patient's Bill of Rights”. The WMA adopted the Declaration of Lisbon in 1981, and amendments were made to it in 1995. It contains 11 principles on patients' rights. In Uzbekistan the law “On the Protection of Citizens' Health” was adopted on 29 August 1996 and came into force on 14 September of that year. The plan: documents of international organisations, the Constitution, the rights of patient and physician, and ethics committees. The aim: to link them with the legislation of Uzbekistan.

t: International organisations and their documents
n: Let us look at international organisations and their documents. The WMA's documents define the duty of the physician, that is, the Declaration of Geneva and the code of medical ethics, and the rights of the patient, that is, the Declaration of Lisbon. In the table, among the WMA documents, are Lisbon 1981 and Helsinki 1975: they concern patients' rights and special committees. In 2000 the WHO prepared guidelines for ethics committees for biomedical research. The UNESCO guide distinguishes four types of bioethics committees. The Council of Europe also has bioethics committees and commissions.

t: The Council of Europe convention: main provisions
n: The main provisions of the Council of Europe convention. The convention was adopted to eliminate the negative consequences of new medical technologies and to protect human rights and dignity. In the area of the genome, a genetic test is carried out only for specified purposes; intervention in the genome is possible only for preventive, therapeutic or diagnostic purposes. In the area of embryos, creating a human embryo for research is prohibited. In transplantology, an organ from a living donor is taken only with his consent and only for treating the recipient. Parts of the body must not be a source of income.

t: Biomedical documents: from Nuremberg to Helsinki
n: Biomedical documents: from Nuremberg to Helsinki. The Nuremberg Code dates from 1947, and its provisions come down to one thesis: for an experiment, voluntary consent and full disclosure of all details are obligatory. The Declaration of Helsinki was adopted at the 18th session of the WMA in June 1964: the interests of subjects always take precedence over the interests of science and society. The declaration was revised several times; the research protocol must be approved by an independent ethics committee. The UN International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, adopted in 1966 and in force since 1976, states that no one shall be subjected to medical or scientific experimentation without his free consent.

t: The Constitution: equality and inviolability (Articles 18–20)
n: The Constitution: equality and inviolability, Articles 18–20. The second section of the Constitution is devoted to the fundamental rights, freedoms and duties of persons and citizens. According to the table, Article 18 establishes equality before the law regardless of sex, race or language. Under Article 19 a right is restricted only by court decision, and lawful rights are inviolable. Article 20 indicates the limit of exercising a right: not harming the interests of others. Right, obligation and responsibility should be understood as inseparable concepts. Citizens have the right to defend their rights in court; this is written in Article 44.

t: The right to life and Article 26: three theses
n: The right to life and Article 26: three theses. Article 24: the right to life is inalienable; Article 25: the right to liberty and personal inviolability. Article 27: protection of honour and dignity, non-interference in private life and inviolability of the dwelling. Article 26 has three parts. The first part is the presumption of innocence, the second the prohibition of torture and degradation of dignity, the third the prohibition of medical or scientific experimentation without consent. Torture is not characteristic of medicine, but the possibility of it is not excluded.

t: Quick question: articles of the Constitution
n: Quick questions on the articles of the Constitution. First question: in which article is the right to life? And the right to personal inviolability? Answer: Article 24 and Article 25. Second question: in which article are protection of honour and inviolability of the dwelling guaranteed? Answer: Article 27. Third question: in which part of Article 26 is the presumption of innocence? And the part on consent? Answer: the first and third parts. Remember: do not confuse the parts of Article 26. Innocence, the prohibition of torture and consent to experiment are not the same.

t: The right to qualified medical care and the state guarantee
n: The right to qualified medical care and the state guarantee. Article 40 guarantees citizens the right to qualified medical care; this means qualified use of all types of help. Article 43: the state secures the rights and freedoms enshrined. This is the state's duty; citizens also have duties to the state. Article 44: judicial protection of rights is guaranteed, with the possibility of appealing to court against unlawful actions of state bodies and officials. Article 45: the rights of minors, persons unable to work and lonely elderly people are under state protection.

t: Duties of citizens: right, obligation, responsibility
n: Duties of citizens: right, obligation, responsibility. Chapter XI of the Constitution is devoted to the duties of citizens. Having a right also presupposes certain duties and obligations. Citizens must observe the Constitution and the laws, respect the rights, honour and dignity of others, and pay taxes and local levies. Citizens must defend Uzbekistan, preserve the historical, spiritual and cultural heritage of the people, and treat the natural environment with care. If duty is not observed, responsibility arises. Therefore right, obligation and responsibility are understood as inseparable concepts.

t: Case analysis: experiment based on consent
n: Case analysis: experiment based on consent. The situation: a researcher, without asking the citizen and without his consent, is carrying out a medical or scientific experiment on him. Question: which norm of the Constitution does this situation violate, and where can the citizen defend his right? Hint: Article 26 of the Constitution has three theses: the presumption of innocence, the prohibition of torture and violence, and the requirement of consent. The citizen can defend his right in court and appeal unlawful actions to a court; this is written in Article 44.

t: History of the patients' rights movement
n: History of the patients' rights movement. In the 1970s a movement for patients' rights began in various countries of the world. The chronology is as follows: in 1972 the American Hospital Association adopted the Patient's Bill of Rights. In 1981 the World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Lisbon. In 1995 an amendment was made to the declaration. The Declaration of Lisbon sets out 11 principles on patients' rights. The declaration has been taken into account in the legislation of most countries, including Uzbekistan.

t: Declaration of Lisbon: principles 1–5
n: Principles 1 to 5 of the Declaration of Lisbon. The World Medical Association adopted the declaration in 1981 and supplemented it in 1995; it has 11 principles. The first principle is quality care: when resources are limited, selection is made on medical criteria, all patients without discrimination. The second principle is free choice: the choice of physician and institution and obtaining a consultation rest with the patient himself. Under the third principle the patient receives information and decides himself. The fourth and fifth principles concern unconscious and legally incapacitated patients. If an unconscious patient has no legal representative, the decision is taken in the patient's interest. A legally incapacitated patient should also, as far as possible, take direct part in the decision.

t: Declaration of Lisbon: principles 6–8
n: Principles 6 to 8 of the Declaration of Lisbon. Treatment against the patient's wish is carried out only in accordance with the principles of medical ethics, in exceptional cases established by law. The patient receives understandable information about his health and medical records, taking account of local culture; he chooses himself the person to whom information is given. Exception: if there are sufficient grounds to believe there is a serious threat to life and health, information may be withheld. Remember: this provision does not fully coincide with the norms of the law. State of health, diagnosis, treatment, prognosis and personal information remain secret after the patient's death. Exception: information about the risk of hereditary disease in descendants.

t: Declaration of Lisbon: principles 9–11
n: Principles 9 to 11 of the Declaration of Lisbon. Everyone is entitled to a healthy way of life, medical care, and sanitary education on prevention and early detection of disease. In the course of care, honour, dignity and the inviolability of private life are respected. The patient has the right to relief of suffering. In an incurable disease the patient has the right to depart from life with dignity and, as far as possible, without pain. He may receive or reject religious support. The Declaration of Lisbon has been taken into account in the health legislation of many countries, including Uzbekistan.

t: Quick question: the Declaration of Lisbon
n: Quick questions on the Declaration of Lisbon. Who adopted the Declaration of Lisbon? The World Medical Association, in 1981; amendments were made to it in 1995. How many principles does it have? 11, from the right to quality care to the right to religious support. Remember: the 4th principle relates to an unconscious patient, and the 5th to a patient unable to make decisions, for example a minor. Under the 5th principle the legal representative gives consent, but the patient should, as far as possible, take the fullest direct part in decision-making.

t: Case analysis: an unconscious patient
n: Case analysis: an unconscious patient. The situation: a patient was brought to hospital unconscious. No legal representative was found, and there is no earlier statement refusing treatment. Principle 4 of the Declaration of Lisbon: in such a case the decision is taken in the interests of the patient. Under Uzbek law, in an urgent case the question is decided by a consilium. If that is impossible, the attending or duty physician decides. Question to the students: who gives consent, and what must the physician do after the decision? Hint: he must inform the management of the institution.

t: The Law “On the Protection of Citizens' Health”
n: The Law “On the Protection of Citizens' Health”. A number of amendments have since been made to the law, but its main content has not changed. The law was adopted on 29.08.1996 and came into force on 14.09.1996. Structure: 6 sections and 47 articles; Article 42 has lost force. Article 13: the right to health protection is inviolable; the state guarantees its protection from discrimination. The first of the five basic principles: observance of human rights in healthcare.

t: Article 24 of the law: patient's rights
n: Article 24 of the law defines the patient's rights. A patient who seeks medical care has the right to respect and compassion. He chooses the physician and the institution, and is treated in conditions that meet sanitary and hygienic requirements. If the patient asks, he makes use of a consilium and consultation with other specialists. He may give voluntary consent to medical intervention or refuse it. The fact of consultation, the diagnosis and information obtained during treatment are kept secret. Insurance, compensation for harm and calling a lawyer are also among the rights. If rights are violated, the patient or his legal representative may submit a complaint to the management of the treatment institution, to a higher administrative body, or to a court.

t: The WHO and the modern model of 1994
n: The WHO and the modern model of 1994. The aim of the WHO is the attainment by all peoples of the highest possible level of health; this is written in Article 1 of the WHO Constitution. In 1994 the WHO formed a modern model of the physician–patient relationship on the basis of three main components: the right to health, the right to information, and the physician's duty. The WHO officially affirmed the principle of giving the patient reliable and understandable information. The physician must explain to the patient everything that interests him and ensure objective, verifiable information.

t: Article 25: the right to information
n: Article 25: the right to information. Every citizen has the right to full information about his state of health, the results of examination and treatment, the diagnosis, prognosis, methods of treatment and their risk. Information about persons under fourteen or recognised as lacking capacity is given to their legal representatives. If an unfavourable course of the disease is anticipated, the information is communicated to the citizen. If he does not forbid it, family members are informed, observing ethical norms. At the citizen's demand, extracts from medical documents reflecting his state of health must be issued to him.

t: Article 26: consent to medical intervention
n: Article 26: consent to medical intervention. Medical intervention is carried out only with the voluntary consent of a citizen who has received information about the illness. The form of consent, written or oral, is not set by law; secondary legislation may determine it. For persons under 14 and those recognised as lacking capacity, the legal representative gives consent. When consent cannot be obtained, the chain is this: there is no possibility of expressing consent, the intervention is urgent, and then a consilium decides. If there is no consilium, the physician decides, and then the management is notified.

t: Articles 27–28: refusal and compulsory care
n: Articles 27 to 28: refusal and compulsory care. A patient or his legal representative may refuse medical intervention or demand its discontinuation; this is in Article 27. The physician obtains written confirmation of the refusal; if that is impossible, a record is drawn up in the presence of witnesses. Article 28: if the disease is dangerous to those around, medical care may be given without consent. Compare: in Article 27 the basis is the patient's will, and the decision rests with the patient or legal representative. In Article 28 the basis is danger to those around, and the decision is made on the ground and in the procedure established by law, for example in dangerous infectious diseases examination, hospitalisation or isolation.

t: Quick question: consent and refusal
n: A quick question on consent and refusal. In which cases may medical intervention be carried out without the patient's consent? Answer within a minute. If the patient cannot express his wish and the intervention is urgent, a consilium decides. If that is impossible, the attending or duty physician decides. If the disease is dangerous to those around, then in the manner established by law, examination, hospitalisation or isolation without consent are possible. Remember: refusal, that is, Article 27, is the patient's right. Compulsory care, that is, Article 28, is linked with danger to those around. Do not confuse them.

t: Medical confidentiality and its exceptions (Article 45)
n: Medical confidentiality and its exceptions, Article 45. Medical confidentiality is preserved after the patient's death; the exceptions are listed in Article 45 of the law. According to the table, the representative of a patient under 14 or lacking capacity may be informed. If the patient cannot express his wish, information is given for examination and treatment. In case of danger to those around, for example in an infectious disease or mass poisoning, the secret may be disclosed. On an official request or suspicion of unlawful harm, information is also given for inquiry, investigation and court. Article 241 of the Criminal Code: failure to report a crime or concealing it entails criminal liability.

t: The Declaration of Lisbon and the law: similarity and difference
n: The Declaration of Lisbon and the law: similarity and difference. Remember: the Declaration of Lisbon is not a law. Ethical requirements have become a norm of law, but do not coincide fully. Paragraph 2 of principle 7 of Lisbon: where there is a serious threat to life, information may be withheld from the patient. Article 25 of the law, by contrast, gives the right to full information; the exception of withholding is not stated. The World Medical Association adopted the declaration in 1981, and it has 11 principles. The law was adopted on 29 August 1996 and has been in force since 14 September; Article 24 has a list of patient's rights. General conclusion: the ideas entered the law, and mostly coincide, but not fully.

t: Three groups of patients' rights
n: Three groups of patients' rights. Patients' rights are conditionally divided by degree of importance into three groups. Basic rights: consent, refusal, information about health and one's rights, medical confidentiality. They are ensured first. Organisational rights: choice of physician and institution, sanitary conditions, compensation for harm; they are linked with the organisation of the service. Additional rights are auxiliary and sometimes not essential: a lawyer, a clergyman, relief of pain.

t: Patients' duties
n: Patients' duties. In practice patients' rights are secured mainly by the actions of medical workers. They can therefore also be seen as the workers' duty. At the same time it is necessary to stress that patients too have duties towards medical workers. The first principle of the law “On the Protection of Citizens' Health” is observance of human rights. In this, the rights of both patient and worker are secured. Patients and those close to them must observe with the workers universal norms of ethics and conduct, and respect their honour and dignity.

t: Case analysis: an infectious disease and refusal
n: Case analysis: an infectious disease and refusal. The situation: a patient suspected of an infectious disease refuses treatment. Question: can he lawfully refuse? Article 27: the patient or his legal representative may refuse intervention. The physician obtains written confirmation of the refusal and, if that is impossible, draws up a record with witnesses. Article 28: if the disease is dangerous to those around, examination, hospitalisation, observation and isolation without consent are possible. This applies especially to infectious diseases. Remember: Article 27 is the right to refuse, while Article 28 is help without consent when danger arises. The existence of danger must be established.

t: Duties of the physician: the Declaration of Geneva and the Code
n: Duties of the physician: the Declaration of Geneva and the Code. Paragraph 1 of the International Code of Medical Ethics: the physician always maintains high professional standards, improves his qualifications, and acquires new knowledge and skills. The physician is honest with the patient and colleagues and fights against incompetent and dishonest colleagues. The pursuit of gain does not affect independent judgement. The physician puts compassion and respect for human dignity first and regards preserving life as a duty. When necessary he gives urgent help to anyone. The Declaration of Geneva, that is, the physicians' oath: lifelong service to humanity, respect for life from its very beginning; not to use knowledge against the laws of humanity.

t: The physician's culture of communication and his rights
n: The physician's culture of communication and his rights. The consultation, state of health and diagnosis are kept secret, including after the patient's death. Herzen: a doctor should have ears but no mouth. In communication it matters not only what is said but how. Shaw: “yes” and “no” are written the same but said differently. Cousins: one should say “three will recover”, not “two will die”. The physician protects his honour, dignity and professional reputation and improves his qualifications. In helping a patient he uses communication and transport free of charge and without hindrance. If there is no trust or the patient does not follow instructions and there is no threat to life, the physician declines: he recommends another specialist and informs the management.

t: Case analysis: a physician who declined treatment
n: Case analysis: a physician who declined treatment. The situation: there is no trust between patient and physician, the patient does not follow the physician's instructions, but there is no threat to his life. Question: in such a case may the physician decline treatment, and how must he then act? Answer: the physician may decline. He recommends another specialist to the patient and informs the management of his institution. Remember: declining is possible only when there is no threat to life. If necessary, urgent help is given to any person.

t: Oncology and the palliative care programme
n: Oncology and the palliative care programme. In Uzbekistan a programme for developing palliative care in the oncology service has been approved. The programme for improving oncological care for 2017 to 2021 was approved in April 2017 by a presidential resolution; its cost is 155 million dollars. Among the indicators, a reduction of the mortality rate from 38.7 to 35 is stated. By 2022 it is planned to open palliative treatment departments in all cancer dispensaries of the republic.

t: The emergence of ethics committees
n: The emergence of ethics committees. The idea was born at the Nuremberg trial, that is, the idea of protecting the human being in experiment. When Beecher's article and the Tuskegee studies became known, the need grew. In the 1960s the first committees appeared in the USA; they consisted only of medical people. In 1975 the Declaration of Helsinki provided for special committees. Then the committees became interdisciplinary: a lawyer, a representative of religion, a psychologist and others joined. In the USA a research act and a National Commission were created; in the 1990s a Presidential Commission. The committees brought bioethics into practice.

t: International organisations and types of committees
n: International organisations and types of committees. In the 1990s an international committee on bioethics was set up under UNESCO. There are also committees in the World Health Organization, the World Medical Association and the Council of Europe. According to the UNESCO guide there may be four types of committees. The first type develops policy and recommendations. The second type is the committee of medical professional associations. The third type is the bioethics committee of medical institutions. The fourth type is the bioethics committee for scientific research.

t: Levels of committees and the experience of countries
n: Levels of committees and the experience of countries. The national committee considers the foundations of policy, the regional committee the problems of the region, and the local committee practical help and the ethical aspects of scientific projects. The structure varies: in the USA Congress created the Presidential Commission, in France a presidential decree created the national committee, in Sweden the government created the committee. France pays attention to the ethics of research, Italy to the safety of biotechnology, Poland to the ethical assessment of laws. In Russia committees have existed since 1987, mainly in scientific research. Modern bioethics consists of 6 parts: academic bioethics, departmental committees, institutional commissions, professional associations, patient associations and movements.

t: Principles of committees and two models
n: Principles of committees and two models. Principles: independence, interdisciplinarity, openness and pluralism, that is, taking account of different opinions. The WHO guidelines, that is, of the World Health Organization, date from 2000 and give the composition of the committee and the procedure of review. An SOP, that is, a standard operating procedure, is the order of steps in the committee's work. There are two models. The American model is more formal, established by law, its decisions are binding in nature, and it has the right to prohibit. The European model is relatively informal, its decisions are more advisory in nature, and it mainly gives recommendations.

t: Ethics committees in Uzbekistan and areas of activity
n: Ethics committees in Uzbekistan and areas of activity. The first bioethics committee was set up under the Ministry of Health; its first head was Academician M.S. Abdullakhodjaeva. Later such a structure was organised under the Ibn Sina International Foundation as well. There is no information on the activity of ethics committees in territorial and local bodies, treatment institutions and scientific organisations. Areas of departmental committees: treatment, clinical trials, education, legislation, organisation of the service, and social, legal and ecological questions.

t: Ethics consultation: 3 models and 3 approaches
n: Ethics consultation: three models and three approaches. Individual consultation is given by one consultant. Broad knowledge and experience are required of him. This model is convenient in an urgent situation but may carry a sign of subjectivity. The small-group model in a simple situation is prompt and more reliable, but subjectivity is not wholly excluded. The ethics committee gives the most reliable, well-founded opinion, but organising it takes time. By outcome, three approaches are distinguished: informative, mediating, that is, oriented to agreement, and directive. In US practice the small-group model is used more often and in many cases is regarded as the most acceptable.

t: Case analysis: resolving an ethical conflict
n: Case analysis: resolving an ethical conflict. First case: in a hospital, in an urgent situation, an ethical dilemma has arisen and a decision is needed at once. Second case: between the patient's relatives and the physicians a complex conflict over values is dragging on, and there is time. According to the source, in an urgent situation individual consultation is convenient, and in a complex conflict the ethics committee is more reliable but takes time. Question: which model and which approach, that is, informative, mediating or directive, suit each of the two cases? Justify.

t: Conclusion: directions for improvement
n: Conclusion: directions for improvement. Article 40 of the Constitution guarantees the right to qualified medical care. The Declaration of Lisbon gives 11 principles of patients' rights. Article 24 of the law “On the Protection of Citizens' Health” defines patients' rights and in the main corresponds to the declaration. The legislation needs to reflect also patients' duties, physicians' rights and their protection. In every health body and institution it is advisable to have an ethics structure: it studies problems in good time.
